title.text:
Regression: explaining
and predicting a number

objects.text: How much does one thing change when another changes, and how well can a model predict it?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 13 of 24  |  Module C: Analyse and explain
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Over the last twelve sessions you learned to load data, clean it, query it, chart it and test whether a gap is more than luck. Today the question gets bigger. When footfall rises, rainfall changes or a promotion runs, how many more orders does a branch get?

That is regression. You will fit a model to the Lakeside Mart weekly data, read every number in it as a sentence, check where it fails, and say what it does not prove.

objects.text: Say what a regression can predict, what it can explain, and what it cannot prove

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can fit a regression line, and a regression with several predictors, by ordinary least squares, and then read each coefficient as one plain sentence for a manager. You can judge the model with residuals, R squared and a residual plot, and you can put a category such as the branch into a model with indicator variables.

And you can say what the model predicts, what it explains, and what it cannot prove. Today is also Project milestone 2, a one page analysis report that you show me for feedback, and you write your project question before you leave.

title.text:
Your two hours: concepts first,
then a Python regression lab

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x2.95_83d54561.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Ideas with pictures first. Then you open the notebook, fit the model and write your one page report.

slides.notes:
We have two hours. The first ten minutes bring back Session 12 and set the question for today. Then forty-five minutes of concepts with no laptops open, so you can follow the pictures. After a ten minute break we open a Colab notebook for the forty-five minute lab.

In every step you predict first, run the cell, read the output and change one thing. The last ten minutes are an exit check and what you keep, including your one page report for Project milestone 2.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  A 95 percent confidence interval for a lift includes zero. What do you tell the manager?
2.  A p-value is tiny. Does that make the effect big?
3.  What does the standard error measure?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 12. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. A 95 percent confidence interval for a lift includes zero. What do you tell the manager?

A good answer is this. We cannot tell yet whether the lift is more than sampling variability. The data are compatible with a gain, with no change and with a loss.

Question two. A p-value is tiny. Does that make the effect big?

A good answer is this. No. The p-value says a gap this size is unlikely if nothing is going on. The effect size says whether the gap matters.

Question three. What does the standard error measure?

A good answer is this. How much a statistic, such as a sample mean, varies from one sample to the next. It shrinks as the sample grows.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 12

rows.text: A 95 percent confidence interval for a lift includes zero. What do you tell the manager?
We cannot tell yet whether the lift is more than sampling variability. The data are compatible with a gain, with no change and with a loss.
A p-value is tiny. Does that make the effect big?
No. The p-value says a gap this size is unlikely if nothing is going on. The effect size says whether the gap matters.
What does the standard error measure?
How much a statistic, such as a sample mean, varies from one sample to the next. It shrinks as the sample grows.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_pin_0.50.png

slides.notes:
Here are the answers to the three warm-up questions. If the interval for a lift includes zero, you tell the manager that the data cannot yet separate a gain from no change or a small loss. A tiny p-value says a gap this big would be rare if nothing were going on, but only the effect size says whether the gap is big enough to matter.

And the standard error measures how much a statistic such as a sample mean varies from sample to sample. Every regression coefficient also comes with a standard error and an interval, so today you use all three ideas again. Which one needed the most thought?

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A model that predicts a numeric target as an intercept plus a weighted sum of predictors. Ordinary least squares (OLS) finds the weights.
The coefficient is the change in the prediction for one more unit of a predictor, with the other predictors held fixed. The intercept is the prediction when every predictor is 0.
Actual value minus predicted value for one record. OLS minimises the sum of the squared residuals.
The share of the variation in the target that the model accounts for, from 0 to 1.
A variable that is 1 when a record belongs to a category and 0 otherwise. One-hot encoding makes one for each level.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_chart_0.63.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.70.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.63.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.63.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_flag_0.63.png

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Regression (linear regression model). A model that predicts a numeric target as an intercept plus a weighted sum of predictors. Ordinary least squares (OLS) finds the weights.

Coefficient and intercept. The coefficient is the change in the prediction for one more unit of a predictor, with the other predictors held fixed. The intercept is the prediction when every predictor is 0.

Residual (prediction error). Actual value minus predicted value for one record. OLS minimises the sum of the squared residuals.

R squared (coefficient of determination). The share of the variation in the target that the model accounts for, from 0 to 1.

Indicator variable (dummy variable). A variable that is 1 when a record belongs to a category and 0 otherwise. One-hot encoding makes one for each level.

title.text:
Regression fits a line through a
cloud: weekly orders against footfall

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_scatter_7.70x4.80_f800e4ae.png
objects.alt: Scatter plot of 832 branch weeks with an upward fitted line

objects.text: A scatter plot has one dot for each record: one branch in one week.

runs.text: 832 dots, one for each record.
Along the bottom: footfall, the predictor (independent variable).
Up the side: orders, the target (dependent variable).

slides.notes:
Today we answer a question you meet at work all the time. When one thing goes up, how much does another change?

In Excel you would draw a scatter chart and add a trendline. That trendline is a regression. Each dot is one record, one Lakeside Mart branch in one week, so there are 832 dots. Footfall, the count at the door, runs along the bottom. It is the predictor, also called the independent variable or the feature.

Orders run up the side. That is the target, also called the dependent variable or the response. The red line is the fitted line, the model. Busy weeks sit high and to the right, and the correlation is 0.84. What would the line tell a manager that the correlation alone does not?

title.text:
The Excel word, the statistics word and
the machine learning word for each part

rows.text: RSQ, or R2 on the trendline

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_chart_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_tag_0.36.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_flag_0.36.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.36.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_notebook_0.36.png

objects.text: LINEST is the Excel function that fits several predictors at once. This course uses predictor and target from here on.

slides.notes:
You already know every part of a regression from Excel, so here is the translation. The trendline on a scatter chart is a linear regression model. The x column is the independent variable, also called the predictor, and in machine learning the feature. The y column is the dependent variable, also called the response, and in machine learning the target.

SLOPE and INTERCEPT give the coefficient and the intercept, which machine learning calls the weights and the bias. RSQ gives R squared. Excel also has LINEST, which fits several predictors at once. From here on I say predictor and target. Which of these words was new to you?

title.text:
Simple linear regression is a formula with
two numbers: an intercept and a coefficient

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.44_7fa5c274.png
objects.alt: Simple linear regression is a formula with two numbers: an intercept and a coefficient

rows.text: The change in the prediction for one more unit of x.

objects.text: 1,000 more people at the door goes with about 18.5 more orders. R squared is 0.706, the correlation 0.84 squared.

slides.notes:
The fitted line is a formula. The predicted target, y hat, equals b zero plus b one times x. B zero is the intercept, the prediction when the predictor is zero. B one is the coefficient, the slope: how much the prediction changes for one more unit of x.

For our data b zero is 1.23 and b one is 0.0185 orders per person. That is a small number, so we multiply by a thousand: a thousand more people at the door goes with about 18.5 more orders. With footfall alone, R squared is 0.706, which equals the correlation squared.

Why would a manager prefer the sentence about a thousand people?

title.text:
A residual is the actual value
minus the predicted value

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_scatter_7.70x4.80_ab147d22.png
objects.alt: Twenty-five weekly records with red segments joining each dot to the fitted line

objects.text: Each red segment is one residual: how far the line misses one record.

runs.text: Residual: e = y minus y-hat. Above the line it is positive.
Gold dot: B01, week of 2024-01-01. Actual 55 orders, predicted 50.8, residual +4.2.
25 of the 832 records are drawn.

slides.notes:
A model is never perfect, so we measure how far it misses. The gap between a dot and the line is the residual, also called the prediction error. It is the actual value minus the predicted value. A dot above the line gives a positive residual. The gold dot is the first record in the file: branch B01, the week of 2024-01-01, with 2,672 people.

The line predicts 50.8 orders, the actual number was 55, so the residual is +4.2. I drew only twenty-five of the eight hundred and thirty-two records so you can see the segments. Is the gold dot above or below the line?

title.text:
Ordinary least squares picks the line with
the smallest sum of squared residuals

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.69_a54602da.png
objects.alt: Ordinary least squares picks the line with the smallest sum of squared residuals

rows.text: Actual and predicted target of record i.
Add the squared residuals of all n records.

objects.text: A rival line with slope 0.015 (and its own best intercept) gives a sum of 47,780. OLS finds the smallest sum: 43,930.

slides.notes:
How does the computer choose the line?

Try any line through the cloud. Every dot sits above or below it, and each gap is a residual. We square every residual so that misses above and below both count, and we add them up. That total is the sum of squared residuals. The method called ordinary least squares, or OLS, finds the b zero and b one that make this sum as small as possible.

A rival line with a slope of 0.015, and its own best intercept, gives 47,780. The OLS line gives 43,930, the smallest possible. Excel does the same thing when you add a trendline. Why do we square the residuals instead of just adding them?

title.text:
Multiple linear regression adds
predictors: footfall, promotion and rainfall

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.33_f619c03c.png
objects.alt: Multiple linear regression adds predictors: footfall, promotion and rainfall

rows.text: promo_on: 1 in a promotion week, 0 otherwise.
rainfall_mm, millimetres of rain in the week.

objects.text: One least squares rule finds all four numbers. statsmodels and scikit-learn give the same numbers as NumPy.

slides.notes:
Real weeks have more than one influence, so we add predictors. This is multiple linear regression: the prediction is an intercept plus one coefficient for each predictor. Multivariate means several targets, so we say multiple. Our model has three predictors: footfall, promo on, which is one in a promotion week, and rainfall in millimetres.

Ordinary least squares finds all four numbers together: 2.38, 0.0188, 6.80 and -0.118. NumPy solves them with matrix algebra, and libraries such as statsmodels and scikit-learn return the same numbers. In your own words, what does the minus sign on rainfall say?

title.text:
Read each coefficient as one sentence,
with its 95 percent confidence interval

rows.text: The starting level. No week has zero footfall (the minimum is 993), so do not read it alone.
1,000 more people at the door goes with 18.8 more orders, other predictors held fixed.
A promotion week has 6.8 more orders than a week without one at the same footfall and rain.
10 mm more rain goes with 1.2 fewer orders, other predictors held fixed.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_key_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_person_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_flag_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_rain_0.50.png

objects.text: Interval = coefficient plus or minus 1.963 standard errors (Student t, 828 degrees of freedom).

slides.notes:
Now the skill your manager cares about: reading each coefficient as a sentence. Footfall: a thousand more people at the door goes with 18.8 more orders, holding promotion and rain fixed. Holding the others fixed is part of the meaning, so always say it. Promotion: a promotion week has 6.8 more orders than a week without one, at the same footfall and rain.

Rainfall: ten millimetres more rain goes with 1.2 fewer orders. Each coefficient has a 95 percent confidence interval, built from its standard error as in Session 12. None of the intervals includes zero. Which sentence would you put on a slide for your manager?

title.text:
R squared is the share of the variation in
the target that the model accounts for

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.77_ce181f3a.png
objects.alt: R squared is the share of the variation in the target that the model accounts for

rows.text: Sum of squared residuals: what the model leaves unexplained.
Total variation of the target around its mean y-bar.
R squared with a penalty for each extra predictor.

objects.text: Footfall alone gave 0.706. RMSE (6.1 orders) is the typical miss, weighting big misses more.

slides.notes:
How good is the fit?

R squared, also called the coefficient of determination, compares two totals. The top is the sum of squared residuals, what the model leaves unexplained, 30,660. The bottom is the total variation of the target around its mean, 149,301. One minus that ratio is 0.795, so the model accounts for about 79 percent of the variation in weekly orders.

Adjusted R squared, 0.794, penalises extra predictors. The root mean squared error, RMSE, is 6.1 orders: the root of the mean squared residual, a typical size of a miss that weights big misses more. For comparison, the same predictors give R squared 0.357 for sales in shillings, because a few huge baskets add variation that footfall cannot explain.

What does an R squared of zero mean?

title.text:
A category enters a regression as indicator
(dummy) variables: one-hot encoding

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_onehot_11.90x4.25_2e47e7e5.png
objects.alt: A category enters a regression as indicator (dummy) variables: one-hot encoding

objects.text: promo_on is already an indicator variable. branch_id has 8 levels, so we make 8 columns and keep 7.

slides.notes:
A regression needs numbers, so a category such as the branch has to be turned into numbers. The standard way is an indicator variable, also called a dummy variable: a column that is one when the record belongs to a category and zero otherwise. Making one such column for every level is called one-hot encoding.

The promotion column is already an indicator. Branch has eight levels, so we get eight columns, and each record has a single one. We keep only seven. The dropped level, B01, becomes the reference level, and the other seven coefficients compare each branch with B01. Why can we drop one column without losing any information?

title.text:
Keep all eight indicators and the intercept and the
model cannot be solved: the dummy variable trap

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_dummy_trap_11.90x4.25_0d9c153e.png
objects.alt: Keep all eight indicators and the intercept and the model cannot be solved: the dummy variable trap

objects.text: Perfect multicollinearity: one column is a copy of the sum of others.

slides.notes:
Here is a classic trap. Put the intercept column and all eight branch indicators into the model. In every row the eight indicators add up to one, which is exactly the intercept column. One column repeats the sum of the others. This is perfect multicollinearity, and it is called the dummy variable trap.

The matrix has 9 columns but its rank is only 8, so many different sets of coefficients fit equally well and the computer cannot choose. The fix is the one you saw on the last slide: drop one level. Libraries such as pandas do this with drop first.

What would the coefficient of the dropped branch be?

title.text:
Seven branch indicators barely change the fit:
R squared 0.796, and adjusted R squared falls

rows.text: Plus 7 branch indicators (B01 is the reference level)

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_chart_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_chart_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_shop_0.50.png

objects.text: R squared never falls when you add a predictor. Adjusted R squared falls when the new predictor adds too little. At the same footfall, promotion and rain, B02 has 0.82 fewer orders than B01.

slides.notes:
Let us see what the branch indicators do. With footfall alone R squared is 0.706. With promotion and rainfall it is 0.795. Adding seven branch indicators lifts it only to 0.796. R squared can never fall when you add a predictor, so it flatters big models. Adjusted R squared charges a penalty for each predictor, and it falls from 0.794 to 0.793.

That is the signal that the branch indicators add too little. The branches differ a little: B02 has 0.82 fewer orders than B01 at the same footfall, promotion and rain. Footfall already carries most of the difference between branches. Would you keep the indicators?

title.text:
A residual plot should show an
even cloud: homoscedasticity

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_scatter_7.70x4.80_261f5bc6.png
objects.alt: Residuals plotted against predicted orders, a cloud that widens to the right

objects.text: Homoscedasticity: the residuals have the same spread at every prediction.

runs.text: Ours grows: standard deviation 5.2, 5.6, then 7.2 orders, low to high thirds.
A fan shape: mild heteroscedasticity.
Intervals for busy weeks are too narrow.

slides.notes:
A residual plot puts the predicted value along the bottom and the residual up the side. If the model is sound, the dots form an even cloud around zero, with the same spread everywhere. That property is called homoscedasticity. Our plot fans out a little to the right.

Split the predictions into three equal groups, from low to high, and the standard deviation of the residuals is 5.2, 5.6 and 7.2 orders. That is mild heteroscedasticity: busy weeks are harder to predict than quiet ones, so a confidence interval that treats every week alike is too narrow for busy weeks.

What would you tell a manager about forecasts for busy weeks?

title.text:
Four patterns in a residual plot
and what to do about each

rows.text: The straight-line model and constant spread look reasonable.
Report the model with its limits.
The relationship is not a straight line.
Add a squared term or change the variable.
The error grows with the size of the prediction.
Model the log of the target, or report wider intervals for large predictions.
A few dots far from the rest
Check those records. Do not delete without a reason.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_chart_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_flag_0.50.png

slides.notes:
Learn to read four patterns. An even cloud around zero means the straight-line model and the constant spread look reasonable. A curve, like a smile, means the true relationship bends, so add a squared term or change the variable. A fan that widens is heteroscedasticity. The error grows with the size of the prediction, so model the log of the target or report wider intervals for large predictions.

And a few dots far from the rest are outliers or data errors, so check those records and never delete them without a reason. Which pattern did our plot show?

title.text:
Prediction: on 208 records it never saw, the regression
misses by 6.3 orders and the baseline model by 14.6

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_bars_7.70x4.80_02c9c0f5.png
objects.alt: Two bars: baseline model misses by 14.6 orders, regression model by 6.3 orders

objects.text: RMSE on the test set: the typical miss on weeks the model never saw.

runs.text: Training set: 624 records, 2024-01-01 to 2025-06-23.
Baseline model: predict the training mean (35.7) every time.

slides.notes:
Explaining is one job. Predicting is another, and it needs a different check. To predict, you score the model on records it never saw. We fit the model on the first seventy-eight weeks, 624 records, which is the training set. Then we predict the last twenty-six weeks, 208 records, the test set.

Splitting by date like this is a time-based split. The baseline model predicts the training mean every time and misses by 14.6 orders. The regression misses by 6.3, close to its training miss of 6.0, and its R squared on the test set is 0.81. Why must the test weeks stay out of the fitting?

title.text:
Explanation and prediction are two
jobs with two ways to check the model

objects.text: Explanation

runs.text: How much does the target change when a predictor changes?
Read the coefficients and intervals.
Check the residual plot.

objects.text: Prediction

runs.text: What will the target be for a new record?
Score the model on records it never saw.
Beat the baseline model.

objects.text: Say which job you are doing before you fit the model.

slides.notes:
Keep the two jobs apart. Explanation asks how much the target changes when a predictor changes. You read coefficients and intervals, and you check the assumptions with a residual plot. Prediction asks what the target will be for a new record. You do not care how pretty the coefficients are.

You score the model on records it never saw, and you check that it beats the baseline model. A model can do one job well and the other badly. A manager who asks for a forecast needs prediction. A manager who asks whether the promotion works needs explanation.

Which job is your own project?

A coefficient depends on the other predictors in the model:
promotion is 5.61 alone and 6.80 with footfall and rain

objects.text: Promotion weeks had slightly lower footfall (1,833 people against 1,910), so footfall hides part of the promotion effect. Rain and footfall are almost unrelated (correlation -0.004), so the rain coefficient hardly moves.

slides.notes:
Here is a warning about reading coefficients. The promotion coefficient is 5.61 when promotion is the only predictor, and 6.80 once footfall and rain are in the model. Promotion weeks had slightly lower footfall, 1,833 people on average against 1,910, so footfall hid part of the promotion effect.

Footfall is related both to the promotion and to orders, so leaving it out changes the promotion coefficient. When a variable is related to both a predictor and the target, it is a confounding variable, a confounder. Rain and footfall are almost unrelated, with a correlation of -0.004, so the rain coefficient barely changes, -0.125 against -0.118.

A coefficient always means: with the other predictors in this model held fixed. Why does that matter when two managers fit different models?

title.text:
A coefficient shows an association,
and a cause needs more evidence

objects.text: What the model supports

runs.text: Promotion weeks go with 6.8 more orders at the same footfall and rain.
Predicting a planned week.

objects.text: What it cannot show

runs.text: That the promotion caused the extra orders.
Nobody randomised the promotion weeks, so a confounder could explain part of the gap.

objects.text: A cause needs an experiment or strong evidence.

slides.notes:
This is the limit of regression. The model supports a statement about association: promotion weeks go with 6.8 more orders at the same footfall and rain. You can use that to predict orders for a planned week. It cannot show that the promotion caused the extra orders. The data does not say how the promotion weeks were chosen, and branches may have run promotions in weeks that were already going to be good.

In Session 12 the loyalty offer was randomised, which is why a lift there could be read as a cause. Here nobody randomised, so a confounder could explain part of the gap. What experiment would settle it?

title.text:
Predict one week by hand: 2,000 people, a
promotion and 20 mm of rain gives 44.3 orders

objects.text: Worked example with the fitted multiple linear regression model.
Question
A branch expects 2,000 people, a promotion week and 20 mm of rain. How many orders?
Working
Answer
About 44 orders. The same week without a promotion gives 37.5.
Check
2,000 lies inside the footfall range of the data (993 to 5,325). Outside that range the prediction is an extrapolation.

slides.notes:
Here is the model at work, by hand. A branch expects two thousand people, a promotion and twenty millimetres of rain. Start with the intercept, 2.378. Add 0.01877 times two thousand, which is 37.54. Add 6.799 for the promotion. Subtract 0.1183 times twenty, which is 2.37. The total is 44.35, about 44 orders.

Without the promotion it would be 37.5. Always check the inputs against the range of the data. Two thousand people is inside the range 993 to 5,325. Predicting for ten thousand people would be extrapolation, and the model has no evidence there. What input would you try next?

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: The intercept is missing, or the numbers are far from the table
X has no column of ones.
Add np.ones(len(bw)) as the first column of X.
X and y have different lengths, or a column is missing.
Print X.shape and y.shape. The rows must match.
Huge coefficients, or a statsmodels multicollinearity note
All 8 indicators and the intercept: the dummy variable trap.
The residual plot shows a wedge
That is the heteroscedasticity from the residual plot slide.
It is a finding. Write it in your report.
statsmodels gives a column named Intercept
The formula adds an intercept for you.
Do not add a column of ones in the formula version.

Five messages you may meet. If the intercept is missing or the numbers are far off, X has no column of ones, so add it as the first column. A ValueError about shapes means X and y have different lengths, so print both shapes. Huge or unstable coefficients, or a multicollinearity note from statsmodels, mean you kept all eight indicators together with the intercept, which is the dummy variable trap, so use drop first and check the matrix rank.

A wedge in the residual plot is a finding, so write it in your report. And the statsmodels formula adds the intercept for you, so do not add a column of ones there. Read the message first. It usually tells you the answer.

rows.text: The promo_on coefficient is 6.8. Say it as one sentence for a manager.

A residual plot fans out to the right. What is the name of the problem, and what does it affect?
Heteroscedasticity. The spread of the errors grows with the prediction, so intervals for large predictions are too narrow.
